topics: 🍷 Wine or Beer? — a blessing begun for the wrong drink: do we follow the opening or the conclusion?
📜 The Ten Commandments — recited in the Temple, but removed from daily prayer 'because of the grievance of the heretics'
🙇 Rav's Teachings via Rabba bar Ḥinnana Sava — Emet VeYatziv, bowing at 'Blessed', HaMelekh HaKadosh, praying for others

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Openings, Conclusions, and What Shema Contains
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 12a–12b
overview.hebrewSource: כְּלָלוֹ שֶׁל דָּבָר: הַכֹּל הוֹלֵךְ אַחַר הַחִתּוּם
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by finishing the analysis of Reish Lakish's 'single blessing' and recalling that the Ten Commandments were once read daily but were abolished to deny the heretics a talking point. The mishna's rule about long and short blessings sparks a famous dilemma: if one began a blessing thinking he held wine and concluded it correctly for beer, does the opening or the conclusion decide? The baraita's 'everything follows the conclusion' is examined and the question is left standing. A chain of teachings from Rav follows — the wording of Emet VeYatziv, how to bow, the Ten Days of Repentance, praying for others, and the atoning power of shame, illustrated by King Saul. The Gemara then explains why the Sages did not add the portion of Balak to Shema and why they did add tzitzit, and a new mishna records Ben Zoma's derivation that the Exodus must be mentioned at night.

slides.title: 🍷 A Blessing Begun for Wine and Finished for Beer
slides.subtitle: Do we follow the essence of the blessing or its conclusion?

nodes.content: ✅ Obvious case: held wine, thought it beer, began intending 'by Whose word all things came to be', concluded 'fruit of the vine' — he fulfilled his obligation, since even shehakol would have worked for wine after the fact
❓ Held beer, thought it wine, began intending 'fruit of the vine', concluded shehakol — do we follow the essence of the blessing (עִיקַּר בְּרָכָה) or the conclusion (חֲתִימָה)?

📜 Come and hear: morning — opened 'Who forms light', closed 'Who brings on evenings' — not fulfilled; opened 'brings on evenings', closed 'forms light' — fulfilled. Evening: the reverse. General rule: everything follows the conclusion

columns.label: Rejection
columns.content: The light blessing is different — it ends with its own full blessing, 'Blessed… Who forms the lights'. Short food blessings have no such closing

columns.label: But per Rabbi Yoḥanan?
columns.content: He says a blessing without mention of God's kingship is no blessing, and the closing lacks it. Answer: since (Rabba bar Ulla) the blessing mentions day and night together, the kingship at the opening covers both

nodes.content: ❓ Then what does 'general rule' add? Not our case — it adds bread and dates: ate dates thinking bread, closed with the dates blessing — fulfilled, since even the bread blessing works for dates, which also sustain. The wine/beer dilemma stays unresolved

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: A proof from a long blessing with its own concluding formula cannot settle a question about a short one-line blessing.

slides.title: 🙇 Rabba bar Ḥinnana Sava in the Name of Rav
slides.subtitle: A chain of practical rulings on prayer and character
rows: Omitting 'True and Firm' in the morning or 'True and Faithful' at night — one has not fulfilled his obligation
'To declare Your kindness in the morning and Your faith in the nights' (Ps. 92:3)
Bow at Barukh, straighten at God's Name
Shmuel: 'The Lord raises the bowed' (Ps. 146:8). 'Before My name he was afraid' (Mal. 2:5) — before, not at. Rav Sheshet bowed like a cane, rose like a snake
Say HaMelekh HaKadosh and HaMelekh HaMishpat instead of the year-round endings
Rabbi Elazar: even 'the holy God' suffices (Isa. 5:16). Rav Yosef sides with him, Rabba with Rav — halakha like Rabba
One who can ask mercy for his fellow and does not is called a sinner
'Far be it from me to sin… by ceasing to pray for you' (I Sam. 12:23). Rava: for a Torah scholar, make yourself ill over him (Ps. 35:13)
One who sins and is ashamed is forgiven all his sins
Ezek. 16:63; proof from an individual — King Saul

slides.title: 😳 King Saul: The Shame That Won Forgiveness
slides.subtitle: Why the proof from Ezekiel is not enough, and where the Gemara finds a better one
slides.hebrewSource: כָּל הָעוֹשֶׂה דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה וּמִתְבַּיֵּישׁ בּוֹ — מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ עַל כָּל עֲוֹנוֹתָיו
slides.label: The argument:
slides.text: Ezekiel's verse speaks to the community, and 'perhaps a community is different' — it is forgiven more easily. So the Gemara turns to Saul before his last battle: he tells Samuel that God no longer answers him 'by prophets or by dreams' (I Sam. 28:15) — but he does not mention the Urim VeTummim. Why? Because he had killed Nov, the city of priests, and was ashamed to consult an oracle that works through a priest. And the shame worked: Samuel says 'tomorrow you and your sons will be with me' — Rabbi Yoḥanan: 'in my company' among the righteous. The Rabbis find the pardon elsewhere: the Gibeonites, who hated Saul, would never have called him 'the chosen of the Lord' (II Sam. 21:6) — a Divine Voice said it.

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: Shame is not a weakness to hide; the Gemara reads it as the sign of true regret that carries atonement.

slides.title: 🦁 Three Portions and the Shape of Shema
slides.subtitle: What was removed, what was never added, and what was included — and why

boxes.title: Ten Commandments — removed
items: Read daily by the priestly watch in the Temple
Shmuel and Rabbi Natan: outside the Temple they sought to read them too, but abolished it because of the grievance of the heretics (תַּרְעוֹמֶת הַמִּינִין)
Rabba bar bar Ḥana in Sura and Ameimar in Neharde'a tried to reinstate them; Rav Ḥisda and Rav Ashi each answered: already abolished

boxes.title: Balak — never added
items: The Sages wanted to include it — not for its mention of the Exodus (usury and weights mention it too)
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin: because of 'He couched, He lay down like a lion… who shall rouse Him?' (Num. 24:9) — an echo of 'when you lie down and when you rise'
Why not that one verse? Tradition: we do not split a portion Moses did not split — and the whole portion would burden the congregation (טוֹרַח צִבּוּר)

boxes.title: Tzitzit — included
items: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ḥaviva: it contains five things — the mitzva of tzitzit, the Exodus, the yoke of mitzvot, and warnings against heresy, licentious thoughts, and idolatry
'After your hearts' = heresy ('the fool said in his heart, there is no God')
'After your eyes' = licentious thoughts (Samson: 'she is upright in my eyes')
'You stray after' = idolatry ('they strayed after the Be'alim')

callout.label: Bonus:
callout.text: Rabbi Ḥelbo: the extra Shabbat blessing was the outgoing watch's wish to the incoming one — 'May He who caused His Name to dwell in this house cause love, brotherhood, peace and friendship to dwell among you'.

slides.title: 🌙 Mentioning the Exodus at Night: Ben Zoma vs. the Sages
slides.subtitle: The mishna and its baraita on 'all the days of your life'

lines.speaker: R' Elazar b. A.
lines.text: I am like a man of seventy, and I never merited to have the Exodus mentioned at night — until Ben Zoma expounded it.

lines.speaker: Ben Zoma
lines.text: 'That you may remember the day you went out of Egypt כֹּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ' (Deut. 16:3). 'The days of your life' — the days; 'all the days of your life' — the nights.

lines.speaker: The Sages
lines.text: 'The days of your life' — this world; 'all' — to include the days of the Messiah.

lines.speaker: Ben Zoma
lines.text: Is the Exodus mentioned in the days of the Messiah? Jeremiah says they will 'no longer say: the Lord lives Who brought Israel up from Egypt', but rather Who brought them from the north country (Jer. 23:7–8)!

lines.speaker: The Sages
lines.text: Not that the Exodus will be uprooted — rather, redemption from the kingdoms will be primary and the Exodus secondary. Likewise 'your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel' (Gen. 35:10)…

callout.label: Where it stands:
callout.text: The Sages read 'no longer' as a shift in emphasis, not erasure; the daf ends mid-sentence with the Jacob/Israel parallel.

summary.principle: A blessing's conclusion decides for long blessings but the short-blessing case stays open; meanwhile the content of Shema and its blessings is shaped by tradition, the fear of heretics, and Ben Zoma's reading of 'all the days of your life'.

flowSteps.content: 🍷 Began for wine, concluded for beer — opening or conclusion? 'Everything follows the conclusion' proves only the long light-blessing; dilemma unresolved
🙇 Rav via Rabba bar Ḥinnana Sava: Emet VeYatziv is essential; bow at Barukh, rise at the Name; HaMelekh HaKadosh in the Ten Days (halakha like Rabba)
😳 Pray for others or be called a sinner; shame atones — Saul avoided the Urim VeTummim and was pardoned ('with me', 'the chosen of the Lord')

columns.content: 📜 Ten Commandments abolished; Balak left out (no splitting Moses' portions, burden on the congregation)
🧵 Tzitzit included — five themes, including warnings against heresy, lust and idolatry

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Ben Zoma — 'all the days of your life' obligates mentioning the Exodus at night; the Sages read 'all' as the Messianic days

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara reject the proof from 'Who forms light / Who brings on evenings' for the wine-and-beer dilemma?
o: Because the light blessing is recited only in the Temple
Because those are long blessings that end with their own concluding blessing, unlike a short food blessing
Because Rav holds that a blessing without God's name is no blessing
Because the baraita's rule applies only to the evening prayer
quiz.e: The Gemara answers 'it is different there, since one says Blessed… Who forms the lights' — a full closing blessing. A short blessing like shehakol has no such independent conclusion, so the case cannot be compared.

quiz.q: What did Rav Ḥisda and Rav Ashi say when Rabba bar bar Ḥana and Ameimar sought to institute daily recitation of the Ten Commandments?
o: That it should be done only in the Temple
That it had already been abolished because of the grievance of the heretics
That it would burden the congregation
That Moses did not divide that portion
quiz.e: Shmuel and Rabbi Natan report that the practice outside the Temple was abolished due to the heretics' grievance, and both later attempts in Sura and Neharde'a were stopped with the same answer.

quiz.q: According to Rav, when does one bow and when does one straighten up during prayer?
o: Bow at God's name, straighten at 'Blessed'
Bow at 'Blessed', straighten at God's name
Bow at the beginning of every blessing and straighten at its end
Bow only at the conclusion of the Amida
quiz.e: Rabba bar Ḥinnana Sava in the name of Rav: he bows at Barukh and straightens at the Name. Shmuel explains from 'The Lord raises the bowed' (Psalms 146:8), and 'before My name he was afraid' teaches humility before, not at, the Name.

quiz.q: Why did the Sages ultimately not include the portion of Balak in Shema, despite the verse 'He couched, He lay down like a lion'?
o: Because it does not mention the Exodus from Egypt
Because Balaam was a gentile prophet
Because one may not read a single verse from a portion Moses did not divide, and the whole portion would burden the congregation
Because it was replaced by the Ten Commandments
quiz.e: The Gemara says reading only that verse is impossible — 'a portion Moses did not divide, we do not divide' — and reciting the entire portion was rejected because of the burden on the congregation (טוֹרַח צִבּוּר).

quiz.q: How does Ben Zoma derive that the Exodus must be mentioned at night?
o: From 'when you lie down and when you rise'
From the extra word 'all' in 'all the days of your life' (Deut. 16:3)
From Jeremiah's prophecy about the north country
From the portion of tzitzit, which mentions the Exodus
quiz.e: Ben Zoma: 'the days of your life' would mean daytime; 'all the days of your life' adds the nights. The Sages instead use 'all' to include the days of the Messiah.
